tagline.text: A neoclassical archdiocesan shrine in the heart of Leganes, Iloilo

location.label: Location
location.text: Leganes town center, Iloilo (Poblacion, around Hilado Street)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (January Saad Festival recommended)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~400 (including round-trip transport from Iloilo City, per person)

children.text: San Vicente Ferrer Church is the main church of Leganes, about 11km north of Iloilo City, and was raised to an archdiocesan shrine in 2008. The building completed in 1889 was rebuilt after the 1948 earthquake, and its neoclassical facade, detached bell tower and stained-glass windows are the main sights.
Leganes is a small municipality just north of Iloilo City, about
11km

away according to Wikipedia. The center of the town's faith and daily life is the Archdiocesan Shrine of Saint Vincent Ferrer. It is both a parish church of the Archdiocese of Jaro and an archdiocesan shrine. Locals usually just call it the Leganes Church.

Many sources trace the town's history to 1858, when the town and parish were organized. It was first named Valencia and soon renamed Leganes. Leganes was a visita of Oton when Fr. Martin Rada founded Oton in 1575, and religious orders such as the Augustinians, Jesuits and Dominicans then took turns running the parish. Work on the stone church began under Fr. Andres Naves around
and was completed under Fr. Eladio Zamora in
. It was built of tabique, brick and bamboo, replacing an earlier chapel made of light materials.

The building went through many trials afterward. A typhoon in May 1896 damaged the church and convent, and around 1898 the parish passed from the religious order to diocesan priests. During World War II the parish records were lost, and on
January 25, 1948

a powerful earthquake that shook Panay (known as the "Lady Caycay" earthquake) destroyed the church. The church standing today was rebuilt from the 1950s, so it is not a fully preserved Spanish-era building; only some remnants survive. One account says a Doric column, a lintel and part of a doorway are traces of the old church.

Even so, the reason this church is a regular stop on Iloilo's church circuit is clear. Archbishop Angel Lagdameo elevated it to a shrine in April 2008, and in September of the same year the Museum of St. Vincent opened to present the parish's heritage and the life of its patron saint. In January the whole town comes alive with the Saad Festival, and this church is where the events begin. It is just the right size for travelers who have seen the churches in Iloilo City (Jaro Cathedral and Molo Church) and want one more.

Fluted pilasters and engaged columns with composite capitals shape the facade. The portico, pediment and front wall carry dentil and molding details, with arched windows. Wikipedia describes the facade as having columns, a central pediment, and arched doors and windows.

The upper facade has volutes that unfurl into acanthus leaves, arches and blind rose windows, and an image of the patron saint is installed there. The pediment shows bas-relief work and a budded cross. From a distance it looks neat and restrained; up close, the texture of the plasterwork stands out.

A large square bell tower stands apart from the main church on the Gospel side (to the right as you face the altar). The bell tower and supplementary buildings are said to have been added during the reconstruction in the 1950s. To fit the whole church in a photo from the plaza, look for an angle that includes the tower.

Inside are vividly colored stained-glass windows said to depict the saint's birth, baptism, the apparition of the Virgin Mary to him, and his death. An oculus in the sanctuary wall is designed so that light falls on the statue of St. Vincent Ferrer.

It has the typical layout of a central nave flanked by two aisles with lower ceilings. A simple altar of Jesus and Mary stands in front of the right aisle, and the baptistery is at the end of the left aisle. If you come during Mass, you can also glimpse everyday life among local worshippers.

A piece of nail and a piece of cloth believed to be connected to the saint are kept in two reliquaries. They used to be displayed for public veneration every first Friday and during the town's fiesta, but this stopped during the pandemic, and they are now said to be kept in a church vault. Ask the parish in advance whether you can see them.

It opened in September 2008 and is said to present the parish's heritage and the life of its patron saint. We could not confirm current opening hours or admission terms, so it is safest to ask the parish before you visit.

blocks.title: Saad Park and the Saad Festival

children.text: Saad Park, near the church, has a life-size statue of St. Vincent Ferrer. The Saad Festival is the town's biggest event, with a Mass at the church followed by a grand parade (Grand Salvo) and street dancing; the street route runs from Saad Park to the festival grounds (Fiesta Pavilion).

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church and a stroll through town

children.text: Take a jeepney bound for Leganes from Jaro Plaza or the Tagbak Terminal in Iloilo City. The ride takes about
30–45 minutes
one way, longer in traffic.
Get off around Leganes Plaza and walk once around the outside of the church. Look at the facade columns, the pediment and the detached bell tower in turn.
If no service is under way, step inside and take your time with the stained glass, the oculus and the altar. During Mass, stay quietly at the back.
Ask at the office whether the Museum of St. Vincent and the relics can be viewed. If not, go see the saint's statue at Saad Park.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town, then head back to Iloilo City.
Avoid taking photos inside the church during Mass or prayer, and ask a priest or guide first.
Start with Jaro Cathedral and Jaro Plaza.
Move on to Molo Church and look at its Gothic-style exterior.
After lunch, head up to Leganes and look around San Vicente Ferrer Church.
If time remains, visit a church toward Santa Barbara, or return to Iloilo City and walk the riverside promenade.
There are several direct flights a day from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Airlines and times change often, so check before booking.
The airport is in Cabatuan, away from Iloilo City. Take a van or taxi from the airport to the city, and check fares locally.

Two jeepney routes between Leganes and Iloilo City are known. The "Leganes–La Paz" route connects Leganes Plaza and La Paz Plaza, and the "Leganes Diversion" route runs between Leganes Plaza and Tanza Cemetery.
According to blog sources, you can board either route toward the Tagbak Terminal or Jaro Plaza. Routes, fares and operating hours can change, so check locally.
It is about
11km
from central Iloilo City, roughly
30 minutes
by car (it varies with traffic). Rather than booking a round trip by taxi or Grab, you can take one one-way and ride a jeepney back.
Within town, walking is enough, and a tricycle works for short distances.
The church and Saad Park are both in the town center, so you can see them on foot.

In the December–May dry season the skies are clear, which suits photographing the church exterior and walking around. The Saad Festival has been fixed in January since 2015, and there is a record of provincial officials attending the January 21 event in 2024, so mid-January onward is recommended if you want to feel the town's energy.
The patron saint's feast is known to fall in early April, but sources give it as April 5 or April 14. It may vary from year to year, so check the parish announcements.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Saad Festival period (January); good for church visits and photos
Around the patron saint's feast (early April); prepare for midday heat
Focus on indoor sights and leave slack in your schedule

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Leganes is a quiet small town, so most visitors stay in Iloilo City. The city has plenty of hotels and hostels, which makes it easy to visit the church as a day trip from your accommodation.

The food is mainly Iloilo's local cuisine. Soups such as La Paz batchoy and bato are famous, but it is hard to vouch for any particular restaurant near this church. Eat lunch in the city before you go, or try local dishes at a restaurant in town.

Visiting outside Mass times lets you see the interior calmly. A weekly notice for November 2026 listed weekday Mass at 6:15–7:15 AM, Saturday morning and 4–5 PM, and Sunday at 6, 7:30 and 9 AM and 4 PM, but times may change, so check.
This is still a place of active worship. Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
The relics and the museum may not be open at all times. If you want to see them, ask the parish office before your trip.
During the Saad Festival in January, roads are closed and crowds gather. Book lodging and transport in advance and start early.
The Spanish-era building collapsed in the 1948 earthquake and the rebuilt church is what you see now; knowing this sets the right expectations.
It works well as a day trip from Iloilo City. Combine it with Jaro Cathedral and Molo Church.
Bring cash (pesos). It is a small town and many places do not accept cards.
During Mass and events, worship comes before sightseeing, and the relics, museum and opening hours may change, so ask the parish before you visit.
The patron saint's feast (sources say April 5 or April 14) and the Saad Festival (January) dates may vary by year, so check the latest announcements.
Avoid loud talking, flash photography and walking across the front of the altar during Mass.
During events, watch for pickpockets and crowds, and keep valuables in front of you.
In the June–November rainy season, typhoons and heavy rain can delay travel. Check the forecast.
The jeepney routes are based on blog sources, so confirm your destination with the driver before boarding.
